# Game of Life, Compiled

Conway's Game of Life has two rules. A live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours stays alive; a dead cell with exactly 3 comes to life. Everything else dies or stays dead. From those two rules come gliders, guns, and patterns that run for thousands of generations before they settle.

This notebook asks a simple question: **how long does a pattern stay busy before the world starts repeating itself?** Every Life world on a finite board must repeat in the end, because there are only so many states. The question is when.

How the cells run:

- **C runs in your browser.** xcc compiles the cell to WebAssembly on the page, so it runs at once, on the website too. It reads the controls with `#include <nb.h>` and shares every generation by printing a `__NB_SET__` line.
- **HTML plays the frames back.** It never works out a generation itself; it only draws what C recorded.
- **JavaScript checks the recording.** It decodes every frame, counts births and deaths, and finds the first repeat.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 1. Pick a start

> Controls, 900 pixels wide: a dropdown "Start with" bound to life_start with R-pentomino alone (rpent), R-pentomino + corner soup (rpent_soup), Glider gun (gun) and Random soup (soup), default rpent; and a slider "Generations" bound to life_gens, 50 to 400, step 10, default 300.

- **R-pentomino**: five cells. On an endless board it takes 1,103 generations to settle.
- **Glider gun**: Gosper's gun, the first pattern found that grows for ever. It fires a glider every 30 generations.
- **Soup**: random cells, 22% of the corners or 35% of the whole board.

After changing a control, press **▶** on the C cell.

## 2. Run Life in C

> In C, run Conway's Game of Life on a 40 by 28 board with a dead border all round. Read the start pattern from nb.life_start with <nb.h> (rpent: an r-pentomino near the middle; rpent_soup: the same plus a 22% sprinkle of cells in the four corners; gun: a Gosper glider gun near the top left; soup: 35% of the whole board) and the number of generations from nb.life_gens (default 300). Use your own seeded random numbers so every run is the same. Pack each generation into hex, 4 cells per digit, row by row, and publish nb.life = {w, h, start, frames} with a `__NB_SET__` line. Print the population at the start, the largest population and when, and at the end.

- **`cur` and `nxt`** are 30×42: the board plus a dead border, so the neighbour count never needs an edge check. The border is a wall: anything that reaches it dies there, unlike the endless board of the textbooks.
- **`emit_frame`** packs 4 cells into one hex digit, so a generation is 280 characters and 300 generations are about 84 KB.
- **`nb_get_string`** reads the dropdown into a buffer and `nb_get_int` reads the slider.

## 3. Play it back

> An HTML canvas that plays nb.life back, 140 ms a frame, looping: live cells blue, cells born this generation brighter, cells that just died as faint ghosts. A scrub bar to jump to any generation (playing stops while you drag), and a line above with the generation, the population and the start pattern. Pick up new frames whenever nb changes. Dark theme.

- **`cellAt`** reads one cell back out of the hex: the digit for cell *i* is `i / 4`, and the bit is `3 − i % 4`.
- Comparing each frame with the one before is what gives the newborn and ghost colours; it costs nothing extra.
Run the C cell above to record generations.

## 4. When does it start repeating?

> In JavaScript, decode every frame of nb.life (4 cells per hex digit) and count the population, the births and the deaths of each generation. Find the first generation whose board is exactly the same as an earlier one, and print when the cycle starts and its period, or say that no repeat came within the run. Return a Vega-Lite chart: generation across, cells up, with lines for population, births and deaths, and a dashed rule where the cycle starts.

- **The repeat test** stores each frame's hex string in a `Map` from text to generation. The first frame already in the map closes the cycle, and the difference between the two generations is its period.
- **Births and deaths** compare each cell with the generation before. Once a world is in a cycle, births and deaths keep happening but balance out.

## What the run shows

- **Five cells keep a 40×28 board busy for 295 generations.** The r-pentomino peaks at 133 live cells at generation 187, then the debris settles. At generation 297 the board is the same as at 295: four still blocks and three blinkers flipping, 25 cells. On an endless board it would run to 1,103; the walls kill the gliders it throws off.
- **Company makes it quieter, not busier.** With the corner soup added, the r-pentomino runs into the debris and the whole board is repeating by generation 73, with 51 cells.
- **Random soup burns out.** 371 random cells thin out to about 100 within 30 generations, and the board freezes completely at generation 239: 18 cells, period 1, nothing moving.
- **The glider gun never settles, but it does repeat.** From generation 49 the board repeats every 60 generations, twice the gun's 30. The gliders crash into the bottom-right corner, and the wreckage takes two gliders to come back to the same shape.
- **Births and deaths never stop in a cycle.** On the chart the green and pink lines keep moving after the dashed line; they just cancel out.

- **A different universe.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Use the HighLife rule instead: a dead cell is also born with 6 neighbours."* Same code, new creatures.
- **Count the gliders.** Press **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** and ask: *"In JavaScript, find every glider in nb.life (the five-cell shape in any of its four phases and four directions) and chart how many there are in each generation."*
